text:
"Transitional commercial," he said.

"Yes."

"Your stall's been here twenty-three years?"

"It has." She set his tea closer. "I made you your first bowl six weeks ago. You ordered without looking at the menu - I thought you were still deciding, but you hadn't looked at it once." She refilled the nearer worker's cup; he took it without a word. "I thought, this one is deciding something else."

That sounded right. He didn't remember the bowl exactly, only the week itself - new enough to the arrangement that he'd been practicing asking for things he wanted before he trusted himself to ask for things he needed. The bowl had been a practice ask. It had worked, and he'd kept coming back.

"The originating complaint numbers," he said. "Do you have them?"

She reached under the counter and brought out a slim folder, rubber-banded, already in order. She'd been expecting someone to ask eventually - not him, not anyone in particular. She just wasn't going to do nothing, and whoever turned out to be useful would need something orderly to work from.

He picked up the folder. "What do you want done?"

She gave him a look that said: what a question. "I want my stall back."

"By end of business today?"

She didn't blink. "If you can manage it."

He paid for the tea, exact. She took the money without ceremony - the deal done, the two of them unchanged, nothing owed either way. He tucked the folder inside his jacket and left without eating. His stomach noted it. He set that aside. He'd get to it.

The originating complaint numbers cross-referenced to three names: Hanna Borg-Okafor, Denis Priyatharan, Sung-Ji Maduka. All three had filed formal hygiene complaints through the zone's citizen portal inside the same six-hour window, all attached to the same petition file number. The petition had thirty-one signatures.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> found a public terminal in the Markel Street transit hall. The civic interfaces were slow and wanted a registration token he didn't have, so he ran the queries through his neuretics instead. The <entity repo="place" guid="945a26fc-6969-5a5b-2737-31fad141a25c">Atlas</entity> array burned through them fast, faster than he could follow, and he'd learned to stay out of its way and wait for the summary.

Hanna Borg-Okafor: address listed as 1140 West <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-c53d-7304-b953-a44879ea410e">Damen</entity>, Unit 3. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> checked the building registry. 1140 West <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-c53d-7304-b953-a44879ea410e">Damen</entity> had no Unit 3. Seven units — 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7, and G, the G a ground-floor storage lock-up on a separate parcel. No Unit 3 had ever existed in the building's records, which ran back to 2198.

Denis Priyatharan: an ID number with a 09 prefix. That prefix went to wards of the zone authority — minors in transitional housing or temporary guardianship. A formal zone-authority complaint required a guardian's signature for any registered minor in the 09 category. There was no guardian signature on the petition. Either the clerk had missed it, or nobody had checked, because nobody expected anyone to look.

Sung-Ji Maduka: address listed as 412 Fulton <entity repo="place" guid="0fb6cf26-aea9-e4d4-06a2-fd40d6bfe217">Corridor</entity>. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> knew 412 Fulton. He'd done a job there in 2224 — a repossession, a contractor debt, clean, nobody hurt. The building had been condemned since 2221, stripped and half torn down. Nobody lived there. Nobody had in five years.

Three complainants. <entity repo="character" guid="019e9e4f-1f20-7486-94ba-e174f3f002c7">Zero</entity> real people.

He sat with that a second longer than the finding required. Somebody had built this the same way he'd build a job — start from the paperwork, work backward from what the reviewer would accept without asking a second question. It was clean work. He recognized clean work when he saw it, because it was the kind he did.

He didn't like recognizing it.

He filed the screenshots to a case folder in his archive and moved to the inspector's report.

Six pages, dense with municipal formatting, printed on AxisMed-grade stock — slightly waxy, slightly bright, the kind that cost three times what it needed to because it read as official. The inspector's name was <entity repo="character" guid="019f3007-f3fc-7cf7-a38d-65c00e100006">Renata</entity> Osei-Bonsu. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> ran it against the zone office's registered inspectors. She wasn't on the West Town list. She was an active contractor for Zone 9 commercial licensing — a different jurisdiction. She'd done four inspections in West Town in the past eighteen months, all for properties that got reclassified afterward.

He sat in the transit hall a moment, tea-shop steam <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aaa1-7cec-8b36-549dcfb312fe">drifting</entity> past from the stall two doors down, the floor thrumming faint under his boots with the <entity repo="corponation" guid="0d831459-182f-4efc-9920-bdf9e032c61d">Pulse</entity> corridor running somewhere beneath the district. Four properties. Not a mistake made once. A tool, used more than once, by someone who knew it worked.

He thought about the folder <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity> had ready before anyone asked her for it. She hadn't known what was coming. She'd just already decided not to be unprepared for it.

He started back toward the stall, because he had thirty-one fake names and one real inspector working the wrong zone, and that wasn't a compliance hold anymore. That was a paper trail with a name on the far end of it, and he intended to find out whose.

The Wentworth <entity repo="place" guid="0fb6cf26-aea9-e4d4-06a2-fd40d6bfe217">Corridor</entity> Development Index took nine minutes to find in the zone authority's public archive, and only because he stopped searching for the phrase and started searching for the amendment number stamped in its footer instead.

It was an internal planning document, not a code. Not enforceable on its own — a projection of which corridors the zone office intended to redraw over the next five years, updated quarterly, filed and forgotten by everyone except the people who'd written it. West Town's transitional-commercial boundary had been redrawn in the version dated three weeks ago. <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity>'s corner sat inside the new line. It hadn't, in the version before that.

He checked the timestamp on the index revision. 09:14, the eleventh.

He checked the timestamp on the recategorization filing against her stall. 09:40, the eleventh.

Twenty-six minutes.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> sat with that number until the tea-shop steam two doors down stopped registering as smell and started registering as time passing. Twenty-six minutes was not a coincidence. Twenty-six minutes was somebody watching a queue, waiting for the index to publish, and firing the filing the moment it cleared — before the ink on the boundary change had time to be anything but private.

He went back to the inspector's report. <entity repo="character" guid="019f3007-f3fc-7cf7-a38d-65c00e100006">Renata</entity> Osei-Bonsu's site visit was timestamped the tenth. The day before the index existed at all.

He read it again to make sure he hadn't misread a date field, the kind of mistake that cost you a case when you took it to someone who'd enjoy finding it. He hadn't. The inspection predated the boundary redraw by nineteen hours. She had walked into <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity>'s stall and written a hygiene violation against a zoning category that would not exist as applied to that corner until the next morning.

Not sloppy. Not early. *Certain.*

Somebody had known the boundary was moving before it moved.

He thought of Osei-Bonsu's Zone 9 registration, four properties reclassified behind her in eighteen months, and felt the shape of it complete itself the way a lock does when the last pin drops — no sound, just the give. Whoever had written the index revision and whoever had sent Osei-Bonsu to that stall were either the same office or two offices that talked to each other before either one talked to anyone required to know. Negligence didn't predict its own paperwork nineteen hours out. Negligence didn't know which corner to hit before the line existed to justify hitting it.

He sat in the transit hall with his tea going cold at a stall he hadn't ordered from and thought about the last time evidence like this hadn't been enough — a ledger he'd handed someone once, complete, dated, unimpeachable, and watched not matter, because the person it was supposed to move already knew and had decided knowing wasn't going to cost them anything. He'd built his life since then on the idea that if you made the proof airtight enough, it would matter regardless of who was looking.

The thought arrived and he let it sit for exactly as long as it took to recognize it was there, then he put it down.

Because sitting with old failures was how you missed current ones.

He had a filing timestamped before its cause. He had an inspector working outside her jurisdiction who'd been right four times running. He had thirty-one names that didn't exist, tied to a report from a woman who'd known where the map would move before the mapmakers signed it.

Whoever this was, they weren't guessing. They were reading something <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> hadn't found yet — a schedule, a feed, a person on the inside of the index office who told them before the quarter closed. And until he found *that*, he had proof of coordination but no name to put on the far end of it, which meant <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity> still didn't have her stall back by end of business, which was the only deadline that had ever mattered in this.

He stood, folder against his ribs, and started back toward Markel at a pace that wasn't quite a walk.

The transit hall's thrumming shifted — the <entity repo="corponation" guid="0d831459-182f-4efc-9920-bdf9e032c61d">Pulse</entity> corridor below cycling into a new routing window. The sound was the same every time, the frequency identical, but <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s array flagged it anyway: something in the subsonic range, just at the edge of perception, a tremor that moved through the building's ferrocrete skeleton and announced itself in his wrists.

He stopped.

The tremor came again. Deliberate. Patterned. Not a transit cycle.

His hand was already moving toward <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> when he saw the woman standing at the corridor entrance forty meters north, in the gap between the tea stall and the defunct elevator shaft. Brown coat. <entity repo="motif" guid="019d6143-a8e1-7cd1-ab7c-1a4110a2ec8c">Hands</entity> visible. <entity repo="archetype" guid="019d6143-a56d-7829-ab88-0be5cc1b1da0">Face</entity> turned slightly away, like she was watching the street and had noticed him only peripherally.

The same woman from the alley behind <entity repo="place" guid="381616e9-d6a3-595d-e865-ce4b15d9310e">The Pivot</entity>.

The same woman from the carousel park.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> didn't move. He let his array catalog her stance — weight balanced, knees slightly bent, the posture of someone who could move in any direction without telegraphing. Not a threat posture yet. Just *ready*.

She turned her head a degree more toward him. Her eyes found his. Held.

Then she raised one hand, slow, palm out. Not a weapon draw. Not a signal. Just: *I'm not coming at you. Not yet.*

She turned back to the street and walked north, into <entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a94e-7740-8aa9-4b82bbd9a223">the Gray Zone</entity> proper, the brown coat disappearing into the pedestrian flow like it had never been solid at all.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> waited. Counted thirty seconds. Sixty. The spot where she'd been stayed empty.

He looked down at the folder in his hands. At the timestamps. At the proof that somebody had known what was coming before it arrived.

Then he looked north, toward the direction she'd walked.

*Not yet*, the gesture had said.

Which meant there was a *when*. Which meant she was moving on a schedule he hadn't seen yet. Which meant that whatever proof he assembled about <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity>'s stall, about Osei-Bonsu and the index revision and the fabricated complaints, was being assembled under a clock that wasn't his to read.

He pulled up his terminal and sent a message to <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity>: *Timeline accelerated. How fast can you move on the <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-a31f-7059-abda-f4a28cc5639c">Halvorsen</entity> chip?*

The response came back in forty-seven seconds: *I work at the speed that keeps me honest. Not faster.*

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> closed the terminal.

He started north anyway, following the route the woman had taken, because she'd shown him her face — the first real acknowledgment that she was watching — and that was either a mistake or a message, and he'd learned a long time ago that people who knew how to move didn't make mistakes.

<entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a94e-7740-8aa9-4b82bbd9a223">The Gray Zone</entity> swallowed him three blocks later, the ferrocrete walls rising higher, the surveillance gaps widening, the city's official structures giving way to the places that ran themselves. The woman in the brown coat was gone.

But the tremor in his wrists stayed. The array kept humming. And somewhere in the data he hadn't found yet, someone was reading a schedule that included his name and his deadline and the exact moment when *yet* became *now*.

The Tessaline <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-c53d-7304-b953-a44879ea410e">Damen</entity> Authentic occupied a corner lot on <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-b3f9-763c-9191-79ee3280bae1">Ashland</entity> where the ferrocrete had cracked enough times that the city had given up on filling it. The storefront was designed to look like it had been there for two hundred years—the kind of lie that required a consultant with a high hourly rate and strong opinions about rounded fonts.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> found <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6ea-1b08-781a-b291-be2c1686aaeb">Mercer</entity> in the back booth, a sales deck hanging in the air over a branded cup. Mid-thirties. The kind of face that had learned to smile at people it had already decided about. When <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> sat down across from him without being invited, <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6ea-1b08-781a-b291-be2c1686aaeb">Mercer</entity> looked up with the patience of someone used to interruptions he considered beneath him.

"This booth is—"

"Garrison <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6ea-1b08-781a-b291-be2c1686aaeb">Mercer</entity>. Franchise coordinator, West Town licensing and real estate." <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> set the folder on the table. "I'm here about the Wentworth Passage compliance hold."

<entity repo="character" guid="019eb6ea-1b08-781a-b291-be2c1686aaeb">Mercer</entity> looked at the folder but didn't open it. He was reading <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> instead—trying to decide whether he was a lawyer, a city official, or just a man who thought he had something. He'd sized up a lot of people this way, and he did it now without seeming to.

"That's a zone authority matter. If you have a concern about the filing, you can direct it to—"

"I have the petition." <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> opened to the first tab. "Hanna Borg-Okafor, 1140 West <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-c53d-7304-b953-a44879ea410e">Damen</entity>, Unit 3. That unit doesn't exist. The building has no Unit 3—no record of one in twenty-eight years." He laid the printout down. "Denis Priyatharan. The ID prefix is 09. That's a minor's classification, and there's no guardian signature on the complaint. Section 12.4 says that signature is required. The complaint is void." He set that page beside the first. "Sung-Ji Maduka, 412 Fulton <entity repo="place" guid="0fb6cf26-aea9-e4d4-06a2-fd40d6bfe217">Corridor</entity>. Condemned in 2221. Torn down to forty percent of the original structure. No registered occupants since." He put down the third page. "Three complainants. None of them real."

He let it sit.

<entity repo="character" guid="019eb6ea-1b08-781a-b291-be2c1686aaeb">Mercer</entity>'s branded cup stood between them, going cold.

The franchise coordinator's jaw moved once—a micro-chew, the kind of thing a person did when they were running calculations too fast to show on their face. His eyes went to the pages and stayed there, cataloging. Not reading. Assessing damage.

"The filing came through standard channels," he said finally. His voice had changed. Softer. "The zone authority processes applications. I don't personally—"

"You signed the intake authorization." <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> turned the petition. There it was: *Garrison <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6ea-1b08-781a-b291-be2c1686aaeb">Mercer</entity>, Coordinator Approval, 2226-03-11 at 14:47.* "Three days before the complaints hit. Before they were filed. Before they existed."

<entity repo="character" guid="019eb6ea-1b08-781a-b291-be2c1686aaeb">Mercer</entity>'s hand reached for the cup. Stopped. He'd just realized that moving would be a tell.

"I process dozens of applications a week. The authorization is—"

"Routine. I know. But here's what's interesting." <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> leaned back. Let him breathe. Let him think he might have room to talk. "The complaints came in through the new batch-processing window. Forty-eight-hour filing cycle, auto-approved if they hit certain keywords. Hygiene violations, capacity concerns, zoning infractions. Your authorization three days *before* that window opened means someone told you what was coming. Someone with access to the filing schedule. Someone who knew the zone authority was running a new protocol that weekend."

<entity repo="character" guid="019eb6ea-1b08-781a-b291-be2c1686aaeb">Mercer</entity>'s eyes went to the door. Calculated distance. Calculated who was in the storefront, in the kitchen, in the back offices of a Tessaline location that had been converted from something else.

"You're making an accusation that requires evidence I don't have access to," he said. His voice had gone very steady. "The kind of accusation that would require—"

"I'm not accusing you of anything." <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> closed the folder. "I'm showing you what I found. What I can show to the zone authority. What I can show to <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity>'s lawyer, if she decides to pursue a civil action for lost revenue and business interference." He stood. "I'm also showing you that whoever put this together knew the system well enough to use it, but not well enough to cover the seam where the authorization predates the event."

He walked to the counter. Ordered tea he didn't want from <entity repo="automaton" guid="019f04f1-58ed-77b6-b3b8-dd17d463bb34">the Noodle Vendor</entity>—the GFA-7 Culinary Service Unit that had been running the same four recipes for thirty-nine years, smiling its mechanical smile at every customer, completely unaware it had a rival fifty meters south.

By the time he turned back, <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6ea-1b08-781a-b291-be2c1686aaeb">Mercer</entity> was standing. The projection had gone dark. The cup had been abandoned. The franchise coordinator's face had settled into the expression of a man who had just realized he was playing a game where the rules had changed without his consent.

"You don't understand how this works," <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6ea-1b08-781a-b291-be2c1686aaeb">Mercer</entity> said.

"I understand that <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity> gets her stall back, or I spend the next week explaining to the zone authority how their new processing window got weaponized." <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> held the tea. It was too hot to drink. "I understand that Osei-Bonsu stops conducting inspections outside her jurisdiction. I understand that the complaints get withdrawn or the system gets audited, and audits tend to be messy for people who've been using the system."

"And if I can't make that happen?"

"Then I assume you're not the person who made this decision, which means I keep looking upstream until I find someone who was."

<entity repo="character" guid="019eb6ea-1b08-781a-b291-be2c1686aaeb">Mercer</entity>'s jaw tightened. The calculation in his eyes shifted—not to escape routes anymore, but to damage assessment. How far up the chain did this go? How exposed was he if the thing he'd signed off on became visible to people with authority?

"The authorization was standard," he said quietly. "I didn't know what it was for. I signed what I was told to sign."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had heard that before. People always said it when they realized they'd been the expendable layer. The one who'd gone first. The one whose signature would be visible on the intake form while whoever had told him to sign it stayed clean.

"Then you're going to want to help <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity> very quickly," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "Because the next person who looks at this is going to assume you did know. And you won't have anyone to pass the problem to."

He walked out of the Tessaline <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-c53d-7304-b953-a44879ea410e">Damen</entity> Authentic without finishing the tea. Behind him, he could feel <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6ea-1b08-781a-b291-be2c1686aaeb">Mercer</entity> doing the math on what it meant to be the visible hand of an invisible decision. How fast the city could turn on you. How quickly evidence became testimony. How the franchise coordinator was about to discover that protecting someone higher than himself required proving he'd been protecting them all along—and that there was no way to do that without destroying his own position.

The tremor in his wrists hadn't stopped. The array was still humming.

But the woman in the brown coat was still gone, which meant the schedule he couldn't read was still running on time.

Which meant *yet* was still counting down.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> pulled up his terminal. Found <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity>'s contact. Sent a new message: *Forget the <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-a31f-7059-abda-f4a28cc5639c">Halvorsen</entity> chip. I need you to pull the filing authorization chain on West Town hygiene complaints, last sixty days. Who signed them. When they signed them. Who they reported to.*

The response came back in ninety-three seconds: *That's not an antiques question anymore.*

*I know.*

*Price has changed.*

*How much?*

*The kind that costs more than money.*

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> closed the terminal and started walking north. Toward <entity repo="place" guid="381616e9-d6a3-595d-e865-ce4b15d9310e">The Pivot</entity>. Toward the place where <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> would be testing something with her hands, not thinking about the fact that her childhood had been stolen by people in offices who thought they were reading schedules nobody else could see.

The brown coat was waiting. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> just hadn't found where yet.

The flour stacks were back by fourteen hundred.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> passed the stall on his way from dropping a document at a zone archive box — an errand that didn't really need doing until the end of the week — and saw them: two white sacks against <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity>'s back wall, the prep bowl right-side up on its shelf, the awning post bare. The compliance notice was gone. The space where it had been taped left a clean rectangle on the glass, a ghost of city-standard red the corridor had already decided to forget. She was moving stock off the supply cart, the one with the wheel that had never been oiled. Her regulars knew that squeak. It meant she was setting up. It meant this was over.

He hadn't come to eat. He'd come to make certain — with his own eyes, at a counter he could sit at without a word passing that mattered — that whatever he'd set in motion this morning had landed clean, that no thread led back to her, that she was safe. He needed the stall open and quiet, and he needed to leave knowing it would stay that way.

He sat at the counter.

She brought him a bowl without asking. Then she cracked an egg over the top — not stirred in, not sunk. Just sitting there on the broth, the yolk whole and bright in the dark, a small sun that hadn't gone under yet. Present.

He paid for the bowl. Exact, the way he always did. She moved the credits aside without counting them and set them on the shelf behind her — not looked at, not questioned, just kept.

She refilled his tea. She looked at his hands — the knuckles first, then the wrists. He looked too. Nothing there.

"You should eat before you do things like that," she said. "Your hands."

"My hands are fine."

"You ate after." She said it like a woman stating a fact she'd already confirmed.

He didn't ask how she knew. He picked up his chopsticks.

The broth was the same as it had been since his first bowl — different in the small daily ways of a thing made by hand, the same underneath. He broke the yolk and let it bleed into the broth, the yellow spreading like a color that had been waiting for permission. He ate the egg. She stood with her cloth and looked out at the corridor, the way she did when she had more to say and hadn't decided whether to say it.

"Twenty-three years is a long time," she said.

He waited.

"When I opened the stall, there was a tea house on the east side of this passage. Three generations of the same family. Good tea — real tea, not concentrate. The kind you had to wait for." She wiped a spot on the counter that was already clean. "A franchise moved in across from them. Then they filed a nuisance complaint. Then a code violation. Then a supply disruption — the delivery route got reclassified, four extra blocks, higher minimum orders, and the tea house couldn't meet them." She folded the cloth and set it down square. "They closed in about fourteen months. The franchise is still there. Different franchise now — the location's been sold twice — but the building's still there."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> set his cup down. He wanted one thing from this conversation before he left: to know whether she was warning him off the corner or asking him to take it. He'd come to hear which, and he wasn't leaving until he had.

"I thought about them this week," she said. "I thought about telling you. Whether it would change how you handled it." She looked at him. "I decided it wouldn't."

"It wouldn't have," he said.

"No." She was quiet a moment. "But it mattered to me. Whether or not it would have changed anything."

He sat with that. Three generations, fourteen months. The corner as it was now, and what it could have been.

"The hold is gone," he said.

"I know." She picked up her cloth. "Eat your bowl."

He ate his bowl. He didn't ask what she'd meant about his hands. She hadn't meant his hands — she'd meant something in him she had no word for, and his hands were where she'd put it. He'd learned not to make her name things before she was ready.

He left exact change on the counter and went home.

title: The Arm Remembers
text:
The door to <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Unit 2E</entity> was open. It always was when she was working — not an invitation, just a permission she'd stopped bothering to withdraw.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> knocked on the frame anyway.

"You didn't eat this morning," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said, without looking up.

"I ate at noon."

"Before noon." She made a small adjustment to something in the vise. "You do better when you eat early. The Atlas burns ahead of schedule when your blood sugar's low. You can't feel it. I can see it in the calibration — your response time drops about four percent." She moved to the next node. "That's not nothing."

The second floor of <entity repo="place" guid="381616e9-d6a3-595d-e865-ce4b15d9310e">The Pivot</entity> smelled like flux and hot metal and machine oil that had soaked into the walls years before either of them got here. Her bench ran the length of the east wall, organized in a way that looked like chaos until you understood the system: tools by frequency of use, components sorted by failure mode, three separate power supplies because redundancy was cheaper than downtime.

He pulled out the second stool and sat.

The thing in the vise was a left forearm. Third-generation pediatric, built somewhere between 2210 and 2215 — old enough to have been through two owners before this one. She had it clamped at an angle that let her reach the wrist actuator without stressing the elbow joint, and she worked with a particular stillness. Not tense. Not loose. Careful, keeping her own hands out of the tool's way.

The actuator housing had a hairline crack along one edge, sealed with putty and left to cure. Clean work, done earlier. The sensor mesh at the wrist was throwing partials, and she was clearing them one node at a time instead of running a full sweep.

He understood why. A full sweep would reset the calibration to factory defaults. She was keeping what was already there.

"Whose is it?" he asked.

"A family in <entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a94e-7740-8aa9-4b82bbd9a223">the gray zone</entity>. The father took a repair shift at a Zone 4 depot — a chain caught him." She held the probe steady over a node. "The girl's nine. They came to me because the AxisMed referral queue is four months and she's growing. The fitting window closes."

"What are you charging them?"

"Materials and half my rate. They're paying in installments." She said it the way she said most things, like it wasn't a decision she'd made.

He looked at the arm. The hardware was good — worn but not failing, the load-bearing parts holding, seals intact. Someone had looked after it. Probably more than one someone.

"The partials," he said.

"Water got in somewhere in its history. I'm working around the dead nodes and rerouting." She held the probe still.

It slipped. Not far, a hair's width, but the node under it flared red and went dark, and three beside it went with it in a cascade she hadn't rerouted for yet. The integrity reading dropped on the bench display. Eighty-seven. Seventy-nine. Seventy-one.

She went very still, then set the probe down with a control that was its own kind of alarm.

"That's a live cluster gone." She pulled the display closer. "Sixty-eight. Under seventy the wrist won't hold fine motor at full range, and I can't rebuild a cluster that's dead. I can only route around it, and I've used the routes I had."

"Can you pull the calibration first?"

"That's the problem. The calibration lives on the same mesh." Her hands hovered above the arm, not touching it yet. "Every route I open to save the range of motion cuts through the sections holding the previous users' data. I save the function, I lose the history. I save the history, it reads under seventy and she gets an arm that fights her." She checked the display again. "I've got maybe two minutes before the mesh finishes settling and decides for me."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> didn't move. "What does she need tomorrow?"

"To not fight it."

She went in.

It wasn't graceful. The stillness turned to something faster and harder — the iron moving in short arcs, the probe trading hands, whole sections of the old mapping opening up and burning off as she cut pathways through them. Twice she stopped mid-motion and took a different angle, salvaging a fragment where a route ran close to one instead of straight through. She didn't explain those. He didn't ask.

At the end of it the display climbed and settled. Eighty-seven.

She set the iron in its stand and stretched her fingers one at a time, the way she did after holding position too long.

"Full range of motion," she said. "The feel will be a little off compared to a clean unit, but she'll adapt faster than she would to a clean one at her age. Kids close that gap in about six weeks."

"And the rest of it?"

"Most of it's gone." She looked at the arm for a moment. "Some isn't. It'll come through as habits the arm already has. Good moves built into the wrist — the way somebody learned to grip a rail, or catch something falling. She won't know where they came from. She'll just be better at those things than she should be."

She picked up a cloth and started cleaning the bench with the same economy she'd used on the arm.

"Your hands were shaking when you came in," she said.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> looked down at them. "They're not now."

"No. They were." She didn't look up from the cloth. She'd read it the way she read everything — off the evidence, not off him. "Rough morning?"

"Yeah."

"I can tell."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> thought about that. Two or three earlier owners, their patterns still in the hardware, handed down to a nine-year-old who'd never know she was inheriting them. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> guiding the new owner through all the old ones.

"You're good at this," he said.

She looked at him — somewhere between modest and unbothered. "I know," she said. She picked up the probe. "There's rice on the counter. Left side."

He found it: a sealed container, still warm. She'd timed it. He ate standing at the counter, because there was no clear surface anywhere else that wasn't holding something that couldn't be moved.

He'd come here for one thing, and he'd been circling it since he walked in. He needed her to pull the full alert history on <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6ea-1b08-781a-b291-be2c1686aaeb">Mercer</entity>'s corridors — every parcel, every recategorization, the whole shape of it — before <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6ea-1b08-781a-b291-be2c1686aaeb">Mercer</entity> noticed the folder had moved and started closing the pattern down. That was the ask. He just had to get to it.

"The hold's gone," he said. "Chen's stall."

"I saw." She adjusted the probe angle. "No trouble?"

"No trouble."

She was quiet. He watched her hands. Then: "The franchise coordinator. <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6ea-1b08-781a-b291-be2c1686aaeb">Mercer</entity>."

"Garrison <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6ea-1b08-781a-b291-be2c1686aaeb">Mercer</entity>."

"Eleven recategorizations in fourteen months. All Tessaline corridors." She said it lightly, like she was reciting something off the top of her head. She wasn't. She'd run the same search <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had — within hours of the hold being filed, because she'd been curious. She hadn't told <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity>, who hadn't asked. She hadn't told <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>, who had the folder. She'd just looked, and kept it, and waited.

"I sent him the folder," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

"I know." She held a node up to the light, turned it, set it down. "The hold came off at thirteen-forty."

"How do you know the time?"

She looked up. "Zone authority posts real-time compliance updates. I have an alert on the parcel."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> took that in. "You have an alert on her parcel number."

"I set it last year. After the Fulton corridor thing." She went back to the probe. "There was a run of coordinated recategorizations along the Fulton commercial stretch — six in eight months, same inspector, two of them closed. I put alerts on a dozen parcels in corridors that fit the pattern. Chen's was one of them."

He hadn't heard about a Fulton corridor thing. He thought about the alert: a quiet line in a system she was already running, going in the background for a year, mentioned to no one. She'd decided <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity>'s parcel was worth watching, and she'd been watching it ever since. He thought about the arm still open in the vise beside her — two or three dead owners' patterns pulled clean and kept, the useful part saved, the rest let go. She did the same thing with information. Kept what mattered. Let the rest run in the dark until it meant something.

"Thank you," he said.

She looked at him. "I'm not doing it for you."

"I know."

She went back to the node. He finished the rice and put the container in the cleaning rack — the routine they'd fallen into over time without either of them planning it. He was reaching for his jacket when she said, without looking up:

"Your door hinge."

He stopped.

"It's dragging when it opens. Not when it closes — just on the open, which means the pin's wearing unevenly. Started about four months ago, I think. Maybe three and a half." She made a small adjustment. "You leave between five-forty and six-twenty most mornings. Come back between twenty-one hundred and midnight on normal days, earlier on contract days with short briefs, later when you're doing prep." She moved the probe to the next node. "The late-afternoon return is unusual. You don't do that often."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> stood with his jacket in his hands.

The hinge had been dragging. He'd noticed it and let it go — it worked, it wasn't urgent. He hadn't mentioned it to anyone. He hadn't mentioned his hours to anyone either. He knew his own rhythms in a rough way, but he'd never counted them out into exact windows.

She had been there. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Across the hall</entity>, working, while the hinge dragged twice a day — once in the morning, once at night — and she'd been listening. Not on purpose. Or not only on purpose. Just there, paying attention, the hinge talking in its small specific way, and her hearing it.

"I can fix it," she said. "<entity repo="character" guid="01a02d38-1757-74fd-8eb3-7e497fc642ab">Five</entity> minutes, if you pull the pin."

"I'll get to it," he said.

She made a small sound that meant: you won't, and we both know it, and that's fine.

He stood in her doorway a moment. The prosthetic arm sat in the vise, the node work two-thirds done, the wrist holding its alignment. The putty on the crack had cured. The arm wasn't new and wouldn't feel new, but it would hold, and the girl would adapt, and in six weeks it wouldn't feel foreign to her at all.

"The arm is good work," he said.

"I know," she said again, the same way — not modest, not performed, just true.

He crossed the hall. His door dragged on the open, and now that she'd named it he could hear exactly what she meant: the catch and release, the uneven wear in the pin, the sound it had been making across four months of mornings without asking anything back. He stood in his apartment with his jacket still on and listened to it.

Tonight he would pull the pin and fix the hinge — not get to it, not someday, but tonight, before he let himself sit down. He'd decided that much standing in her doorway, though he hadn't said it out loud. It was a small thing to owe himself, and he wanted it done.

He thought about the tea house — three generations, fourteen months, a corner that was now a second franchise doing nothing much. <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity>'s hands on the counter cloth, the extra egg, the way she'd said it: twenty-three years, as if saying it out loud made it more real. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s hands on the prosthetic node, patient and exact, keeping what was already there. An alert running quietly in the background for a year, no credit asked for.

He took his jacket off and hung it by the door.

<entity repo="weapon" guid="4ab24f74-61d4-4f45-b326-7c6b98c96279">Cacophony</entity> sat on the side table. He checked <entity repo="weapon" guid="4ab24f74-61d4-4f45-b326-7c6b98c96279">the cylinder</entity> out of habit. Six rounds, where they had always been. He went to the kitchen and put the kettle on. He hadn't had enough tea, and the evening still had some hours in it. Tonight he wanted only to close the day out clean - put the folder to bed, empty the cup, and let the hours run down to nothing without spending a single thing he didn't have to.

The hinge was quiet with the door closed.

From <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">across the hall</entity> came the faint sound of <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> working - the probe tool, the soft pulse of calibration software, the small sound of her moving the lamp. The nine-year-old would have her arm by the end of the week. The gap would close in six weeks, and she'd stop noticing the arm as a separate thing. It would just become part of how she moved.

Other nights her side of the hall stayed dark instead, no probe tool, no lamp, and that told him something too - a different rhythm, one he wasn't part of and had never asked to be. A crew of women she danced with on Thursdays at a bar in <entity repo="place" guid="019ef735-1581-7998-9cfa-2c6411898545">the Bloom Quarter</entity> he'd never once been invited to. A card circle that kept no fixed schedule and answered to no name he knew. She never explained the absences and never apologized for them, and he never asked, because asking would have made it a thing that needed his permission, and it plainly didn't. He'd come to understand, without either of them saying so, that a closed, dark door <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">across the hall</entity> could mean nothing was wrong at all - that this, too, was a kind of trust, maybe the realest kind: the space to not be accounted for.

He poured his tea and carried it to the window. Below, the corridor did its evening business: a shift change at the AxisMed supply depot, <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-04fb-7227-94d9-6b4d889ce52b">Boost</entity>'s crew at the corner in a setup they thought was subtle and that <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> could read at two hundred meters, a maintenance mech moving in smooth silence where the squeaky one had been earlier. Someone had oiled the wheel, or the mech had done it itself, or the work had happened the way it sometimes did in this city - somebody paying attention, quietly, filing no report.

The folder was on the side table. Three names that weren't people, a building code that didn't apply, a timestamp proving the fraud was planned before its excuse existed. He'd spent an afternoon on it. He'd file the copy in his case archive at the weekend and forget it. <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6ea-1b08-781a-b291-be2c1686aaeb">Mercer</entity> would find easier corridors, probably without much trouble. That wasn't <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s problem.

<entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity>'s stall was on Wentworth Passage. It had been there twenty-three years. He'd been coming to it for six weeks.

Wentworth Passage. He set the tea down before he'd finished the thought, because the thought didn't want finishing. The building code that didn't apply. It didn't apply to the address on the folder - a lot on the north end of the market district, permits pulled for a structure that wasn't there yet. He knew that block. He'd walked it a thousand times. The fraud wasn't aimed at some corridor he'd never see. <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6ea-1b08-781a-b291-be2c1686aaeb">Mercer</entity>'s easier corridors ran straight through the passage where <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity> had stood for twenty-three years, and the timestamp said the clearing had been decided months ago, dressed up as a code violation after the fact. The stall wasn't in the paperwork. It didn't need to be. It was just in the way.

He drank his tea until it was gone. It didn't help.

The <entity repo="place" guid="945a26fc-6969-5a5b-2737-31fad141a25c">Atlas</entity> array was quiet. He could feel the overclock pulled back, the processing down at maintenance level, no red edge behind his eyes. A day that hadn't cost him much. Nothing had needed spending. The weapons had stayed where they were.

He set the cup in the cleaning rack.

He went to bed earlier than usual - because he'd eaten, because the folder was filed, because nothing tonight needed him awake to finish it.

In the morning he would leave between five-forty and six-twenty.

The hinge would drag on the open.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Across the hall</entity>, someone would hear it, and know he was on his way, and say nothing, and have the rice warm by the time he came home.
